questions.title: Complement a complete DFA
questions.question: Construct a complete DFA over {0,1} for words NOT matching 11(0|1)*01. Use prefix states P0,P1, tail states T0,T1,T2, and rejecting-error state X of the original positive-language DFA. Which final set should the complemented DFA have?
questions.explanation: First complete the positive-language DFA, then swap final and nonfinal membership for every state. Its old rejecting sink must become accepting too.
worked_solution: The positive-language DFA has only T2 final. Its complete state set is {P0,P1,T0,T1,T2,X}.
The complement uses all states except T2 as finals: {P0,P1,T0,T1,X}. It includes ε and words too short to match the original regex.

questions.title: Design a DFA for modular symbol counts
questions.question: Build a DFA over {0,1} whose number of 1 symbols has residue in {0} modulo 3. Let qr mean residue r and start at q0. After 101101, which state and verdict are correct?
questions.explanation: Count the specified symbol, not total length or the binary numeric value.
worked_solution: State r records the count modulo 3. Reading 1 increments it modulo 3; reading the other bit leaves it unchanged.
The input has 4 occurrences of 1, so its remainder is 1. The final residues are {0}.

questions.title: Construct an NFA for a prefix and suffix
questions.question: Construct an NFA for abΣ*ba over Σ={a,b}. Keep the fixed prefix and suffix nonoverlapping. Use it to classify these words: 1: abba; 2: aba; 3: ababa; 4: abbaa.
questions.explanation: The middle state both loops on the alphabet and nondeterministically starts the suffix path when its first symbol appears.
worked_solution: First build a path spelling ab. At its endpoint add a loop for every alphabet symbol and a separate path spelling ba to the only final state.
All missing NFA transitions have destination set ∅. A branch accepting early cannot ignore remaining input.
abba: accept
aba: reject
ababa: accept
abbaa: reject

questions.title: Construct an NFA for repeated alternative blocks
questions.question: Construct an ε-NFA for (001|110)*. Classify: 1: ε; 2: 001110; 3: 00; 4: 0011100. Treat each parenthesized alternative as a complete block.

worked_solution: Use s as the only final state. Add ε edges to the beginning of each separate block path; return to s by ε only after a whole block is consumed.
Each block has length 3. This supplies a quick necessary length check, but the symbols within each block still matter.

questions.title: Construct an NFA for a modular OR
questions.question: Over {a,b}, accept when the a count has residue in {1} modulo 3, OR the b count has residue in {0} modulo 2. Construct an ε-NFA with two counting branches and classify: 1: ε; 2: aaaabbb; 3: aaabb; 4: aabb.
questions.explanation: Each branch checks one condition on the same whole input. An accepting branch suffices, including when both conditions hold.
worked_solution: From fresh s, ε-branch to A0 and B0. A states count a modulo 3 and loop on b; B states count b modulo 2 and loop on a.

aaabb: remainders (0,0); accept

questions.title: Choose a representation to prove regularity
questions.question: Use the equivalence theorem to prove that words over {0,1} with length congruent to 1 modulo 2 form a regular language. Choose an exact regex; R^k here would mean k concatenated copies, not Kleene star.
questions.explanation: The construction in the worked solution preserves exactly the required words.
worked_solution: Let B=(0|1), describing one arbitrary alphabet symbol. Use 1 leading copies, then any number of groups of 2 copies.
The lengths are exactly 1+2k for k≥0. Every word of such a length can be divided this way.
The constructed regular expression specifies precisely the target, so the equivalence theorem implies the language is regular. A remainder DFA gives an alternative proof.

questions.title: Avoid drawing a huge length DFA
questions.question: Over a fixed finite nonempty alphabet, words must have length divisible by 4, 6 AND 9. Leading positions have no other restrictions and ε is allowed. Select the exact expression and justify regularity.
questions.explanation: The required block length is the least common multiple, which need not equal the product when the divisors share factors.
worked_solution: lcm(4, 6, 9)=36. A length satisfies all three divisibilities exactly when it is a multiple of 36.
Σ^36 is a fixed concatenation of a finite regular symbol language; its star is regular.
Equivalently, intersect the three regular multiple-length languages. A DFA can track length modulo 36, but drawing it is unnecessary.

questions.title: Eliminate two interior GNFA states
questions.question: The GNFA below has start s and sole final f. Unlisted edges mean ∅. Eliminate p first and q second, keeping direct alternatives and loops. Which regex describes the complete language?
questions.explanation: The construction in the worked solution preserves exactly the required words.
worked_solution: After removing p: s→q becomes (b)|(a)(b)*(a); s→f becomes (ε)|(a)(b)*(b). The q loop and q→f remain unchanged.
After removing q, append the through-q term ((b)|(a)(b)*(a))(b)*(a) to the existing s→f alternative.
The result is (ε)|(a)(b)*(b)|((b)|(a)(b)*(a))(b)*(a). Since s has no incoming edge and f no outgoing edge, this sole final edge is the answer.

questions.title: Eliminate with loops and return edges

questions.title: Minimize a complete DFA by partition refinement
questions.question: Minimize the complete DFA below. First remove unreachable states, then show the initial final/nonfinal partition and every strict refinement. How many states remain in the minimal reachable complete DFA?
questions.explanation: Equivalent states agree on every continuation. The proof of minimality uses distinguishing suffixes between every pair of distinct quotient states.

Partition 0: {0A,0B,1A,1B} | {2A,2B}
Partition 1: {0A,0B} | {1A,1B} | {2A,2B}
The final partition is stable. Each block becomes one state:
Minimality check: each pair of distinct quotient states has a distinguishing suffix. C0/C1: 1; C0/C2: ε; C1/C2: ε.

questions.title: Pump equal constrained symbol counts
questions.question: Prove nonregularity of L={w∈{0,1}*:|w|0=|w|1=n^2 for some integer n≥1}. Assume pumping length p≥1 and choose w=0^(p^2)1^(p^2). For an arbitrary legal split w=xyz, which k=2 conclusion supplies the contradiction?

options.label: |xy^2z|0=p^2+d and |xy^2z|1=p^2, where 1≤d≤p; unequal counts violate L.
Choose y=ε; pumping deletes all the 0s.
y must contain equal numbers of 0s and 1s, so pumping is impossible.
Both counts become p^2+d, so they are unequal.

questions.explanation: The chosen zero block has at least p symbols. Every legal y lies entirely in it and has positive length, so pumping changes only the zero count.
worked_solution: Suppose L is regular, and let p≥1 be its pumping length.
The witness w belongs to L by taking n=p, and its length is at least p.
Let w=xyz be any split with |xy|≤p and |y|>0. Since the first p^2 symbols are 0 and p^2≥p, y=0^d for some 1≤d≤p.
Choose k=2. The pumped word has p^2+d zeros and p^2 ones. They are unequal, so no value of n can satisfy the definition.
This contradicts the pumping lemma for every legal split. Thus L is not regular.

questions.title: Pump a unary power-length language
questions.question: L={a^(n^2):n≥1}. Assume pumping length p≥1 and choose w=a^(p^2). Every legal y=a^d has 1≤d≤p. Which k=2 conclusion proves the pumped length is not a square?

options.label: Every nonempty unary language is nonregular.

questions.explanation: The next square is 2p+1 symbols farther away, which exceeds the maximum d=p.
questions.sources: S05 pp. 4, 9, 11-12; transfer practice from S01 Q10
worked_solution: Assume regularity and let p be a pumping length. Choose the stated witness, which belongs to L and has length at least p.
For any legal split, the length of y is d with 1≤d≤p. At k=2, the new length is p^2+d.
The gap (p+1)^2-p^2 equals 2p+1, which is greater than p≥d.
Therefore the new length lies strictly between consecutive integer squares. It is outside L for every legal split, a contradiction.

worked_solution: Suppose L regular. Pick w=a^(2^p), which belongs to L and is long enough.

questions.explanation: Use |xy^kz|=q+(k-1)d, then factor and verify that both factors exceed one.

worked_solution: Choose a prime q satisfying q≥p+2; primes are unbounded. The witness a^q is in L and has length at least p.
For an arbitrary legal split, 1≤d≤p. The unpumped xz portion has length q-d.
At k=q-d, the length is q+(k-1)d=(q-d)(d+1).
Here q-d≥2 and d+1≥2.
Thus the new length is a product of integers greater than one, not prime. This contradicts the pumping lemma for every legal split.

questions.title: Repair the quantifier error in a false proof
questions.question: A student claims (aa)* is nonregular: "Let p≥2 be a pumping length; choose w=a^(2p), x=ε, y=a, z=a^(2p-1). Pumping k=0 gives odd length, so the language is nonregular." What is the decisive error?

options.label: The word a^(2p) is not in (aa)*.
One failing split is insufficient; the legal split x=ε, y=aa, z=a^(2p-2) pumps within (aa)* for every k≥0.
The pumping segment must always have length exactly p.

questions.explanation: A regular language only needs some good split of each sufficiently long word. The proposed proof must defeat every legal split, not just its chosen bad one.
worked_solution: The chosen word is a valid member and k=0 is allowed. Those are not the errors.
With y=aa, |xy|=2≤p and |y|>0. The length after pumping is 2p+2(k-1), an even nonnegative number for every k≥0.
This legal split defeats the attempted contradiction. Independently, (aa)* is itself a regex, so its language is regular.

questions.title: Repair an invalid pumping witness
questions.question: For L={a^n b^n:n≥0}, a proposed proof chooses w=a^p b^(p+1) and forces y into the a block. What is the necessary first repair?

options.label: Choose a witness in L, such as a^p b^p, before applying the lemma.
Keep the witness because only its length matters.
Assume p=1 because pumping lengths are chosen by the prover.
Set y=ε to balance the counts.

questions.explanation: The lemma applies only to words in the assumed-regular language. The proposed witness has unequal counts, so the lemma promises nothing about it.
worked_solution: First assume L regular and let p be its pumping length.
Use w=a^p b^p, which is both in L and at least p symbols long.
For every legal split, y=a^d with 1≤d≤p. Pumping k=2 gives a^(p+d)b^p, outside L. Now the contradiction is valid.
